name: Hassan Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a formwork carpenter, lead hand on a crew of six for a concrete subcontractor, and right now we're on a twelve-storey apartment block on Harbour Road. I'm on site by half six, check the props and the deck from the day before, then we build the forms for the next floor so the concrete can be poured. I love pour days, honestly, when the truck turns up and everything's square. What wears me out is the weather, my knees, and the paperwork the main contractor keeps sending.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how do you get by on the money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My girlfriend Priya, she's a nurse on the heart ward at the city hospital. We rent a two-bedroom flat about twenty minutes from site and we've got about four months of bills put away, which we're trying to grow into a deposit. I'm also the union rep for our crew, which mostly means chasing overtime rates and making sure the young lads get their breaks. I don't use any of the AI stuff, never have; Priya sets up half the apps on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying for years: what matters on site is the concrete, the timber and the people. If the office saves an hour on paperwork, good for them. I'd probably post in the union group chat that we should stop worrying about robots and start talking about pay again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief. I'm not great with screens, and I've been half-waiting for someone to tell me I need an app to do my job. If nothing changes, my worries are the old ones: rent going up, my knees, and whether Priya and I ever get a deposit together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on running my crew on the Harbour Road job, which has another eighteen months of floors to pour. I'd keep putting about 300 a month into the deposit account. And at the next union meeting I'd push for the heat-stress breaks we've been asking for, because summers on a deck keep getting worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest, because a few people told me I was a dinosaur for not using the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned rent going up. How much of a squeeze is that right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It went up 80 a month in March, and the landlord's hinting at more. We're fine, we've got the four months put by, but every rise pushes the deposit further off. I can hang a formwork deck in the rain at seven in the morning, but I can't make a landlord stop raising the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you think about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny, our youngest. He's nineteen and on an apprentice wage. Nothing in this picture hurts him, but nothing helps him either, so I'd just want him to finish his ticket and get proper pay.

say: I'd tell people **the site** is still about concrete, timber and people, not software.
I'd steer the **union chat** back to pay instead of robots.
think: Privately I'd feel **relieved**, because I'm slow with screens and dreaded needing an app.
My real worries stay the old ones: **rent rises**, my knees and our deposit.
do: Keep running the **formwork crew** on the Harbour Road tower for its last eighteen months.
Put about **300 a month** into the deposit account with Priya.
Push for **heat-stress breaks** at the next union meeting.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a touch of smugness about never using the tools.
S0.quote: I can hang a formwork deck in the rain at seven in the morning, but I can't make a landlord stop raising the rent.
fieldNote: His work feels **secure**; the only pressure he names is **rent**, eating into the deposit.
He measures the world through the **crew**, especially the apprentice Danny.
Being proved right about AI hype matters to him more than he admits.

steps.text: Keep running the formwork crew on the Harbour Road tower
Put 300 a month into the flat deposit account
Push for heat-stress breaks at the next union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the site's still the site, you can't email a slab into place. In the union chat I'd tell people to watch the office side, because that's where jobs will go quietly: the estimators, the schedulers, the people who order the materials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry the planning side of my own job gets taken off me. Right now I read the drawings, work out where the props go and order the ply. If a program does that, I'm just the bloke who carries it out, and that's a pay cut waiting to happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my head down and keep the crew tight, that's the first thing. I'd ask the union to get something in writing about who checks the computer's prop layouts, because if a layout is wrong it's my lads under that deck. I wouldn't go learning the software myself, not unless they made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not scared for my hands yet, I'm more annoyed that the part of the job that uses my head might go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the software unless they made you. What if they did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do the course and grumble the whole way through. I'd rather check a prop layout with a tape and my own eyes than trust a screen that's never stood under wet concrete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm fine for now, which is true. She'd probably say the hospital's already got AI doing the nurses' rotas and nobody died. She's more relaxed about it than me.

say: I'd say **the site** can't be run by email, so hands-on jobs stay.
I'd warn the union chat that **office jobs** like estimators go first, and quietly.
think: I fear losing the **planning** part of my job: drawings, prop layouts and ordering.
If software plans and I only build, that looks like a **pay cut** coming.
do: Keep the **crew** tight and keep my head down on the tower job.
Ask the union for a written rule on who **checks** computer prop layouts.
Avoid learning the **planning software** unless the firm makes it compulsory.
feel: **Uneasy** and a little annoyed that the thinking part of his job may go first.
S1.quote: I'd rather check a prop layout with a tape and my own eyes than trust a screen that's never stood under wet concrete.
fieldNote: He sees clearly that his **lead-hand pay** rests on the planning work, not the lifting.
His answer to change is a **union rule**, not a new skill.
Safety, not money, is the argument he reaches for first.

steps.text: Keep the six-person formwork crew together on the tower job
Ask the union for a written rule on checking computer prop layouts
Hold off learning the planning software until the firm requires it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that this needs rules, fast. Somebody has to decide who gets paid when a machine does the work, and it shouldn't just be the developers. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd write to my local representative, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking stuff, then robots for formwork around 2031, when I'd be thirty-two. Formwork is the same thing again and again, deck after deck, and that's exactly what a robot would learn first. I think I'd be out of a trade before I've even bought a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start saving harder now, 500 a month instead of 300, even if it means fewer nights out. Push the union for a fund that pays builders to retrain. And I'd hold off on the flat, because I don't want a mortgage tied to a job that has five years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if I'm honest. And angry, because nobody asked people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on the flat. How would Priya take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. She's been looking at listings on her lunch breaks for a year. Nursing's hands-on too, so she'd have the same three years as me, maybe more, and we'd probably end up still renting after a long talk at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between the thinking AI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be three good years of pay, maybe better pay, because the bosses would be rushing to finish jobs before everything changed. But I'd spend them knowing what was coming. Three years of overtime with a robot on the way is not a career, it's a countdown.

say: I'd demand **rules** on who gets paid when machines do the work.
I'd go to every union meeting and write to my **local representative** for the first time.
think: Repeat formwork is exactly what **robots** learn first, around **2031**.
I expect to lose my trade at **thirty-two**, before we've even bought a flat.
do: Raise savings from 300 to **500 a month** by cutting nights out.
Push the union for a **retraining fund** for builders.
Put off the **flat purchase** so no mortgage hangs on a dying job.
feel: **Frightened** about his trade and **angry** that workers had no say.
S2.quote: Three years of overtime with a robot on the way is not a career, it's a countdown.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his trade** within five years, which is why the mood is alarmed.
The three-year robot gap reads to him as a **countdown**, not breathing room.
He turns to **collective action** and politics before any personal retraining plan.
Putting off the flat will cost him at home with **Priya**.

steps.text: Raise deposit savings from 300 to 500 a month
Push the union for a paid retraining fund for builders
Write to the local representative about rules for site robots
Put off buying a flat with Priya

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, really: we need rules. I'd sound calmer, though, because five years is time to get organised. I'd be telling the younger lads to join the union now while it still has teeth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the AI, three more for the robots, so I'd be about thirty-five before formwork goes. That's time to save a real cushion. What I still don't know is what I'd do instead, and that's the part that sits in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and save about 400 a month. Get our union branch to set up a committee on site robots and put my name down for it. Maybe study for a supervisor's ticket, because someone has to sign off on what the machines build, at least at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the fast one. More of a slow worry than a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you're not good with new technology. How would a supervisor's ticket work for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the contradiction, I know. I'd hate the screen side of it. But I know concrete better than anyone on our site, and a supervisor who knows concrete is worth something even if a robot's doing the lifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which plan would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday. Priya and I were going to see her family next summer, and I'd cut it to a week to save. Five years sounds like a lot until you count how many pay packets that really is.

say: I'd still call for **rules**, but more calmly, with time to organise.
I'd tell the younger lads to **join the union** while it has teeth.
think: Formwork would last until I'm about **thirty-five**, time for a real cushion.
Not knowing **what I'd do instead** is what really worries me.
do: Save about **400 a month** and cut next summer's trip to a week.
Join a union **committee** on site robots.
Study for a **supervisor's ticket** so I can sign off machine work.
feel: **Anxious**, but as a slow worry rather than a panic.
S3.quote: Five years sounds like a lot until you count how many pay packets that really is.
fieldNote: Five years gives him a **cushion** but no picture of a **next job**.
He admits the gap between hating screens and wanting a **supervisor** role.
His concrete knowledge is the asset he leans on.

steps.text: Save 400 a month toward a bigger cushion
Join the union branch committee on site robots
Study for a site supervisor's ticket
Cut next summer's family trip to one week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it properly, with the government paying for retraining instead of leaving it to each of us. Ten years is long enough for the unions to win something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years plus three for the robots, I'd be forty. Half a career. I'd probably buy the flat, have a few good years, and then hit the wall in my forties, which might be worse in a way. Starting over at forty with a mortgage scares me more than starting over at thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy the flat with Priya in the next two years, probably. Keep a bigger cushion than we planned, six months instead of four. Stay in the union and keep pushing, but I wouldn't jump trades now, there's no point leaving good work early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anxious. There's time, but I know I'm the type who leaves things too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think you'd leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I always do. I didn't get a smartphone until everyone else had one for years. My dad always said I'd be late to my own funeral, and he's usually right about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing one of those robots actually hang a deck or tie steel on a real site, not in a video. If I saw that with my own eyes, I'd sign up for a course the next month.

say: I'd say a decade is time for **state-paid retraining**, not everyone alone.
I'd tell people the **unions** can win something real in ten years.
think: Robots would reach formwork when I'm about **forty**, half a career in.
Starting over at forty **with a mortgage** scares me more than at thirty.
do: Buy the **flat** with Priya within two years.
Grow the cushion from four to **six months** of bills.
Stay in my trade and keep **pushing the union**, with no early jump.
feel: **Uneasy**, knowing he tends to act **too late**.
S4.quote: My dad always said I'd be late to my own funeral, and he's usually right about me.
fieldNote: With ten years his job is **safe for now**, so the worry sits further off.
He sees a **mortgage at forty** as its own trap.
He says only **seeing** a working robot would make him act.

steps.text: Buy a flat with Priya within two years
Build the cushion up to six months of bills
Keep pushing the union for state-paid retraining
Wait to see a working site robot before starting a course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough for anything, and formwork's the kind of repeat work a robot would learn first. What would help is a proper retraining fund that pays a wage while you learn, run with the unions, not some website full of videos. If a robot takes my job, the money it saves should pay for my next one, not for the developer's next boat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Safety. Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, but nobody asks who's responsible when one drops a panel off the tenth floor. I'd want that sorted before anything else.

headlineQuote: If a robot takes my job, the money it saves should pay for my next one, not for the developer's next boat.
portrait: **Hassan** is a 27-year-old **formwork lead hand** on a twelve-storey apartment block and his crew's union rep.
He rents with his girlfriend **Priya**, a nurse, with about **four months** saved toward a deposit.
He avoids **new technology** and trusts his tape and eyes over any screen.
He is calm in **AI Plateau** but sees repeat formwork as easy work for robots in the AGI pictures.
His answer to every picture is **union rules** and public retraining more than a personal plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because formwork robots by 2031 would end his trade at **thirty-two**.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining fund** that pays a wage while he learns, run with the unions.
Clear rules on **who is responsible** when a site robot causes an accident.
